items.prompt: In cache-lib, which operations refresh an entry's last-use reading?

options.text: Only set, when it adds a new key
options.rationale: A new entry starts with a fresh reading, but reads refresh it too.

options.text: get, and set on a key that is already cached
options.rationale: Both call touch with the current clock reading.
Writing an existing key also calls touch.

options.text: None: the Map's insertion order tracks recency
options.rationale: The Map order is never changed after insertion; recency is the lastUsed field.

items.prompt: Why does LruCache take a clock function instead of calling Date.now() itself?
items.modelAnswer: So a test can pass a fake ticking clock and know every reading, which makes the results deterministic.

items.prompt: Explain to a new contributor how cache-lib knows which entry was used least recently.

required.idea: Each entry stores the clock reading of its last use

items.modelAnswer: Each entry stores lastUsed, the clock reading of its last use, and get and set call touch to refresh it, so the smallest lastUsed belongs to the entry used longest ago.

items.prompt: A cache with capacity 3 holds 3 keys. You set one of those keys to a new value. How many entries are dropped?
items.explanation: set returns early for a key it already holds; evict is only called before adding a new key.

options.text: On every set once the cache has ever been full
options.rationale: An update of an existing key returns before the capacity check.

options.text: Before adding a key it does not hold, when size has reached capacity
options.rationale: The check runs first, then the new entry goes in.

options.text: After inserting, when size is above capacity
options.rationale: The size never goes above capacity: the check runs before the insert.

options.text: On get, when the cache is full
options.rationale: get never drops anything; it only refreshes recency.

items.prompt: Explain when cache-lib drops an entry and when it does not.

required.idea: Only when adding a new key
And only when the cache is full

misconceptions.description: Updating an existing key drops an entry

items.modelAnswer: It drops one entry only when you add a new key while the cache is already at capacity; updating a key it already holds just refreshes it.

items.prompt: Capacity 2, and the clock returns 1, 2, 3 and so on, one step per call. You set a, set b, get a, then set c. What lastUsed reading does the entry a correct LRU cache drops have?
items.explanation: a is read at 3, b was last used at 2, so b (reading 2) is the least recently used.

items.prompt: Read LruCache.evict as it is written. With capacity 2: set a, set b, get a, set c. Which key does this code drop, and why?

required.idea: Because it keeps the entry with the largest reading, the most recent one

items.modelAnswer: It drops a, because the comparison keeps the entry with the largest lastUsed, which is the most recent one.

items.prompt: Explain to a friend which entry a least-recently-used cache should drop, and how evict can find it in one pass.

required.idea: The entry with the smallest last-use reading
Keep the best candidate while walking every entry

items.modelAnswer: It should drop the entry with the smallest lastUsed, the one used longest ago. evict can loop over each entry once and keep the one with the smallest reading so far.

items.prompt: Explain your fix to evict: what was wrong, and what would break if the comparison were flipped back?

required.idea: evict must keep the entry with the smallest reading
Flipped back, it drops the entry just used and the first test fails

misconceptions.description: Dropping the newest entry is correct

items.modelAnswer: evict kept the largest lastUsed; it must keep the smallest, the least recent entry. Flipped back, it drops the entry just used and the first test fails.
